title: Ancestral Visions of the Future review – visceral cine-memoir is a haunting return to Lesotho
excerpt: Lemohang Jeremiah Mosese pairs his literary-grade voiceover with propulsive, prophetic images to interrogate his identity and that of his colonialism-carved homeland
content_html:
Here is a captivating stream of consciousness film about exile, roots and identity by Lemohang Jeremiah Mosese, director of the lauded 2019 activism story This Is Not a Burial, It’s a Resurrection. It’s ostensibly a cine-memoir looking back from the vantage point of present-day Berlin to his upbringing in Lesotho, narrated by Mosese’s dense, literary-grade voiceover. But there’s something propulsive and prophetic about the accompanying hyper-vivid images from rural and urban life. This is something more than memory.

The title screen dedication is ambiguous: “This film is an ode to cinema, an eternal no to my mother.” Reneging on the title of another 2019 work, Mother, I Am Suffocating. This Is My Last Film About You, she is central to Mosese’s attempt to return to the source. Her aspirations are to keep her family well-dressed and out of poverty, carry them away from the grind of rural fields that “ask not for rain, but for blood”, and see them installed in an ever-expanding house in the city (presumably Maseru).

Ancestral Visions of the Future touches peripherally on colonialism, the hand that shaped this landscape. Perhaps the roll of red fabric that extends down the hillsides is meant to evoke the scalpel that carved up the country “like meat on the map”. Instead of a linear perspective, Mosese proposes an African conception of time as a cycle – and lets it erupt in bursts of ecstatic and pained mysticism. After a sequence of endless toil on the furrows, an old farmer plucks out his own eyes and plants them. The young boy alongside him harvests the crop, “allowing him to see everything”.

Mosese’s vision clouds in the face of cyclical urban forces. He recounts his failed career as a street switchblade thug, then the tragedy of a woman burned alive by a lynch mob when her baby unknowingly “shoplifted” an item. Seen baying like a wildcat in front of invisible foes, she appears to be another sacrificial victim in an eternally recurring drama of violence and victimisation. More inspirational is the example of Sobo, a martial artist, herbalist and puppeteer he meets in Maseru in later life, who can see “not the city as it is, but the city as it is becoming”.

Mosese seems to be seeking the same visionary capacity – and maybe something more: perhaps redemption, for Lesotho, or himself? Or even, guided by the unfiltered energies here, direction towards a kind of rejuvenation. Whatever the exact meaning, this intense homecoming leaves a scorched trail in its wake.

content_html_zh:
这是一部关于流亡、根源和身份的迷人意识流电影，由 Lemohang Jeremiah Mosese 执导，他执导了 2019 年备受赞誉的激进主义故事《这不是埋葬，这是复活》。 这表面上是一部电影回忆录，从当今柏林的角度回顾他在莱索托的成长经历，由摩西浓密的文学级画外音讲述。 但随之而来的来自农村和城市生活的超生动图像却具有某种推动力和预言性。 这不仅仅是记忆。

标题屏幕的奉献语含糊不清：“这部电影是对电影的颂歌，是对我母亲永远的拒绝。” 背弃了另一部 2019 年作品《妈妈，我快窒息了》的标题。 这是我关于你的最后一部电影，她是摩西试图回归源头的核心。 她的愿望是让家人穿得体面，摆脱贫困，让他们远离“不求雨水，只求鲜血”的农村田地的辛劳，并看到他们在城市（大概是马塞卢）一座不断扩建的房子里安顿下来。

《祖先对未来的愿景》外围地触及了殖民主义，即塑造这片土地的那只手。 也许沿着山坡延伸的红色织物卷是为了让人想起“像地图上的肉一样”分割这个国家的手术刀。 摩西提出了一种非洲的时间概念，而不是线性视角，而是一个循环，并让它爆发出阵阵狂喜和痛苦的神秘主义。 经过一系列无休止的犁沟劳作后，一位老农夫挖出了自己的眼睛并把它们种在了地上。 和他一起收割庄稼的小男孩“让他看到了一切”。

面对周期性的城市力量，摩西的愿景变得模糊。 他讲述了自己作为一名街头弹簧刀暴徒的失败职业生涯，以及一名妇女因孩子在不知情的情况下“偷窃”一件物品而被私刑暴徒活活烧死的悲剧。 她像野猫一样在看不见的敌人面前狂吠，她似乎是一场不断上演的暴力和受害戏剧中的另一个牺牲品。 更鼓舞人心的是索博的例子，他是一位武术家、草药师和木偶师，他晚年在马塞卢遇到了他，他看到的“不是城市的本来面目，而是城市正在成为的样子”。

摩西似乎正在寻求同样的远见能力——也许还有更多：也许是对莱索托或他自己的救赎？ 或者甚至，在此处未经过滤的能量的引导下，走向某种复兴的方向。 无论确切的含义是什么，这种强烈的返乡之旅都留下了焦黑的痕迹。
